metaDescription: Four electric snow blowers at or under $200 compared on motor amps, clearing width and depth, throw distance and cord versus battery for small driveways.
expertTake: The Westinghouse WSnow20 is the best overall pick under $200 because its 1800 watt motor, 20 inch path and a known brand cover walkways and short driveways. The 15 amp 18 inch unit is the value pick for narrow paths. Anyone clearing more than a few inches of wet snow on a long drive should skip this band and buy a larger single-stage or two-stage machine.
introParagraphs: At this price, a snow blower is a plug-in or small cordless machine meant for walkways, decks, steps and short paved driveways. It trades the reach and power of a gas blower for light weight, easy starting and no fuel to store.

Prices move, and the $200 cap reflects listing prices when this guide was updated. This guide explains what a corded blower can and cannot do, how to read clearing width and depth, and ranks four machines by who they suit, with honest limits on snow depth and wetness.

products.name: Westinghouse WSnow20 20-Inch Corded Electric Snow Blower 1800W
products.description:
The Westinghouse WSnow20 is a corded single-stage blower with a 20 inch path, a 120V 15 amp 1800 watt motor and a rubber-tipped steel auger. The maker says it throws 680 pounds of snow per minute and can reach 25 feet, and dual LED lights help with early morning clearing. A 7 inch intake depth suits fresh snow on pavement.

The tradeoff is the cord and the depth. A corded machine ties you to an outlet and an extension cord, and 7 inches is the practical limit before the auger starts packing. Compared with the generic 20 inch machine in this guide it offers a recognized brand and clear specifications, and compared with a cordless shovel it moves much more snow.

Ownership is simple: clear the chute with a stick, never with a hand, check the cord for nicks and store the machine dry. Use a heavy-gauge extension cord rated for the amperage. A good routine is to start at the outlet end, throw the snow away from the cord and work outward in overlapping strips, so you never run over the cable. In very cold weather the rubber cord stiffens, so uncoil it indoors first and keep the plug connection lifted out of slush with a simple hook or a loop of tape.
products.bestFor: Short paved driveways and walkways with an outlet nearby.
cons: Limited to about 7 inches of snow

products.name: 15A 20-Inch Corded Electric Snow Blower 25 ft Throw Dual LED
products.description:
This unbranded 20 inch blower lists a 15 amp motor, a two-blade steel auger that clears a 21 inch wide by 12 inch deep path and a claimed 800 pounds of snow per minute. A 180 degree adjustable chute throws snow up to 25 feet, and dual LED lights extend the working hours.

The tradeoff is brand support and honesty of the numbers. A 12 inch depth claim from a 15 amp motor is optimistic, since the auger on a single-stage electric struggles beyond about 8 inches of light snow, and an unbranded seller offers thin service. Compared with the Westinghouse it gives a slightly wider path but less assurance. The extra inch of width also means a heavier intake, so the motor bogs sooner in dense snow, and the wide housing is harder to turn on a narrow path. If you choose it, buy for the sake of fewer passes on a broad walk rather than for more capacity per minute.

Use light passes, clear the chute with a tool and keep the cord behind you. Because the listing claims a depth that its motor will not sustain, treat the first storm as a test: take shallow passes at half the claimed depth, listen for the motor slowing and note how far the snow actually flies. If it performs well, a 20 inch machine is a pleasant way to clear a wide walk, and if not, the return window is the time to find out.
products.bestFor: Wider walks where an outlet is close.

products.name: 15A 18-Inch Corded Electric Snow Blower 25 ft Throw Dual LED
products.description:
The 18 inch version has a two-blade steel auger that clears a path 18 inches wide and 9 inches deep, with a 15 amp motor and a claimed 800 pounds of snow per minute. It shares the 180 degree chute and dual LED lights of the larger model but is lighter and easier to turn on narrow paths.

The tradeoff is width. An 18 inch path takes more passes on a driveway, and a narrow body is the point on a porch or a narrow walk. Compared with the 20 inch unit it is more nimble, and compared with the Westinghouse it has a narrower path and less brand backing.

Store it dry, check the paddle and shear hardware and use a short heavy cord. A narrow machine is also kinder to the person pushing it: the lower weight makes turning at the end of a pass easy, and the smaller intake means the motor rarely bogs. Many owners keep an 18 inch blower for steps and the front walk and a shovel for the corners the machine cannot reach, which is a sensible division of labor.
products.bestFor: Narrow walks, steps and small decks.

products.name: MZK 20V 13-Inch Cordless Snow Shovel With Directional Plate
products.description:
The MZK cordless snow shovel clears a 13 inch wide path up to 6 inches deep and runs on a 20V battery, with an adjustable directional plate that controls where the snow lands. It needs no cord, which is its main advantage on steps, decks and cars.

The tradeoff is scale. A snow shovel is not a blower: it covers a narrow strip and runs for minutes on a battery. Compared with the corded blowers it moves far less snow but goes anywhere. Compared with the unbranded corded units it adds mobility at the price of capacity.

Charge the battery indoors, store it at partial charge and keep the auger clear of ice. Because the tool is so small, it makes sense to clear the car and steps first, where its strengths lie, and leave the driveway to a larger machine or a shovel, a division that gets the most out of a modest battery and keeps frustration low. Use it for light dustings rather than wet snow. Wet snow is heavy, so a small battery will drain in minutes, and the auger can pack and stall on slush. If your area gets a lot of heavy, wet snow, a shovel-type tool is a supplement to hand shoveling and not a replacement for it, and the battery should be kept warm in a coat pocket or indoors until you start.
products.bestFor: Steps, decks and small paths without an outlet.

buyingCriteria.criterion: What electric single-stage blowers can do
buyingCriteria.explanation: A single-stage electric blower uses a rubber-tipped auger that touches the pavement and throws snow itself, with a typical throw of 10 to 25 feet. It suits paved walks and short drives and snow up to roughly 6 to 8 inches. A two-stage machine feeds snow to a separate impeller and handles deep, heavy snow, but it costs far more. If your driveway is over about 60 feet or the snow is routinely deeper than 8 inches, an electric blower in this band will be a frustration. Set expectations before you buy, because the number one complaint is a machine asked to do a bigger job than it was built for. A fair test is the weight of the snow: six inches of fluffy powder weighs very little, while six inches of wet, heavy snow can weigh several times more per shovelful and will stall a small motor. Check the forecast type for your region, because the difference between powder and slush is the difference between a happy and a disappointed owner.

The Westinghouse lists a 120V 15 amp 1800 watt motor, and the generic units list 15 amps. That is the practical limit of a household outlet. A 15 amp motor needs a heavy-gauge extension cord, 14 gauge or thicker and as short as practical, because a thin or long cord starves the motor and can overheat. Plan your cord route so the cord stays behind you, and keep the plug connection off the snow with a cord retainer or a loop. Use only an outdoor-rated cord marked for cold weather, and plug into a GFCI outlet if one is available, since snow and moisture around a connection create a shock risk. Never use a cord with damaged insulation, and unplug the machine before you do anything to the auger or the chute.

The Westinghouse lists a 20 inch width, the generic 20 inch unit a 21 inch by 12 inch path and the 18 inch unit an 18 by 9 inch path. Width sets passes, and depth sets how much snow the auger can swallow. Depth numbers on small electric machines are often optimistic, so treat 6 to 8 inches as a safe working range and plan to clear in two passes after a big fall. The first pass skims the top half and the second reaches the pavement, which keeps the motor from bogging and gives a cleaner finish. Clearing snow while it is still falling, rather than waiting for the storm to end, is the habit that makes small electric machines work well.

Corded machines give unlimited runtime at the cost of a cord. Cordless machines such as the MZK shovel move freely but run on a small battery and handle very little snow. In this price band, cordless means a shovel-type tool, not a true blower. If your driveway is short and an outlet is nearby, corded wins on capacity. If you only clear steps and a car, cordless wins on convenience.

A rubber-tipped steel auger, as on the Westinghouse, protects pavement and improves grip. A 180 degree adjustable chute lets you change discharge direction without turning the machine. Check that the chute control can be reached with gloves and that the chute cleaning tool is stored on the machine. Never clear a jam with your hand, even with the motor off. The auger stores spring energy and can turn after the motor stops, and injuries from hand clearing are one of the most common snow blower accidents. Keep the clearing tool tied to the handle, wear boots with good grip and clear the area of children and pets before you start, because thrown snow can hide stones and toys.

Dual LED lights help with dawn and dusk clearing, and low weight helps on steps and turning. Electric blowers store flat and need no fuel, which is a big advantage for small garages. Check the folding handle, because a blower that stands upright in a corner is more likely to be used than one that must be dragged out from under a pile of boxes. Keep the machine near the door you use, not at the back of the shed, because the first snow of the season is often the one that catches you unprepared. Also keep a spare shear pin or paddle bolt in a labeled bag, since a small plastic part is the usual cause of a machine that will not clear on a morning when you need it.

howWeEvaluated.title: Clearing capability
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared motor amps, clearing width and stated depth. The Westinghouse's 20 inch path and 1800 watt motor set the benchmark. Depth claims on generic units were treated with caution.

howWeEvaluated.title: Power system
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared corded power against a 20V battery. Corded units scored for runtime and the shovel scored for freedom. Cord handling and heavy-gauge extension needs were noted.

howWeEvaluated.title: Design and control
howWeEvaluated.description: We looked at chute adjustment, lights and auger design. Adjustable chutes and rubber-tipped augers scored higher. Units without details lost points.

howWeEvaluated.title: Brand and support
howWeEvaluated.description: We considered the maker's reputation and published specifications. The Westinghouse listed clearer specs. Unbranded units scored lower for support, since a buyer who needs a replacement paddle or a new switch has nowhere to turn but the seller, and the likelihood of finding parts a few seasons later is small.

howWeEvaluated.title: Fit for the budget
howWeEvaluated.description: We matched each machine to a likely user, from narrow walks to a short driveway. No machine in this band was credited for jobs beyond a few inches of light snow.

cards.label: Blower
cards.text: The Westinghouse and generic corded machines move hundreds of pounds of snow per minute and throw it to the side. They need a cord.

cards.label: Shovel
cards.text: The MZK cordless shovel is battery powered and goes anywhere but clears a narrow strip of light snow.

howToChoose.note: Choose a blower for a driveway and a shovel for steps.

rows: Outlet at the edge of the walk

cards.label: Look for
cards.text: Look for a rubber-tipped auger, an adjustable chute, a heavy-gauge cord and a handle that folds. Clear snow as it falls rather than waiting for a deep pile, and use light overlapping passes.

cards.label: In this comparison
cards.text: The Westinghouse WSnow20 is the best match for light snow on pavement. The 18 inch machine is best for narrow areas.

cards.label: Spend more if
cards.text: Spend more if your driveway is long, your snow is deep or wet or you cannot run a cord. A cordless single-stage blower or a gas machine is the right tool beyond this price.

cards.label: Save if
cards.text: Save if you only clear steps and a short walk a few times a winter. Any of these is enough.

maintenance.why: A nicked or thin cord is a fire and shock risk. Replace damaged cords.

maintenance.task: Clear the chute with a tool
maintenance.why: Never use a hand. Turn off and unplug before clearing a jam.
Worn rubber loses grip and throws less snow.
Moisture rusts fasteners and damages the motor.

faq.q: Is $200 enough for a snow blower?
faq.a: For light snow on a short paved driveway, yes. Prices move, and the cap reflects listing prices when the guide was updated. For deep snow, budget much more.

faq.q: How deep a snowfall can it handle?
faq.a: About 6 to 8 inches of light snow. Maker depth claims of 9 to 12 inches are optimistic. Take two passes after a big fall.

faq.q: Can I use any extension cord?
faq.a: No. Use a heavy-gauge cord, 14 gauge or thicker, rated for outdoor use and kept short. A thin cord overheats.
No. The auger can throw stones. Use it only on paved surfaces.
For steps and a car, yes. It clears a narrow strip and runs for minutes. It is not a driveway tool.

faq.q: How do I clear a jam?
faq.a: Turn off and unplug the machine and use the clearing tool. Never use your hand. Let the auger stop fully.
